q: In the sentence "The nurse placed a warm blanket over the shivering patient," what part of speech is the word "over"?
w: "Over" links its object, "the shivering patient," to the verb "placed," showing where the blanket went, so it is a preposition.

n.0: "Over" would be an adverb only with no object after it ("The aide came over"); here it has the object "patient."
n.1: "Shivering" is the adjective describing "patient"; "over" shows a relationship of place.
n.3: A conjunction joins words or clauses; "over" introduces a noun phrase, not a clause.

q: In the sentence "The infection cleared, but the cough lingered for two more weeks," what part of speech is the word "but"?
w: "But" joins two independent clauses ("The infection cleared" and "the cough lingered"), so it is a coordinating conjunction.

n.0: An interjection stands apart to show feeling; "but" connects the two halves of the sentence.
n.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "but" links two complete thoughts.
n.3: "But" is a preposition only when it means "except" and takes an object ("everyone but Sam"); here it joins two clauses.

q: In the sentence "Well, your blood pressure looks better than it did last week," what part of speech is the word "Well"?
w: Set off by a comma at the start of the sentence, "Well" expresses a reaction and has no grammatical link to the rest of the sentence, so it is an interjection.

n.0: A conjunction joins words or clauses; "Well" joins nothing and stands apart at the start of the sentence.
n.1: "Well" is an adjective when it means healthy ("I feel well"); here it describes no noun.
n.3: "Well" is an adverb when it tells how something is done ("works well"); here it modifies no verb.

q: In the sentence "The patient's heart was beating fast during the stress test," what part of speech is the word "fast"?
w: "Fast" tells how the heart was beating, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb. The same spelling is an adjective in "a fast pulse," so the word's job decides.

n.0: "Fast" would be an adjective before a noun ("a fast heartbeat"); here it modifies the verb "was beating."
n.1: The verb is "was beating"; "fast" describes the beating.
n.3: "Fast" is a noun only when it names a period without food; here it tells how something happened.

q: In the sentence "Yesterday was the busiest day of the month at the clinic," what part of speech is the word "Yesterday"?
w: "Yesterday" is the subject of "was" and names a day, so it is a noun here. In "She called yesterday," the same word is an adverb.

n.0: "Yesterday" is an adverb when it tells when an action happened ("She called yesterday"); here it is the subject.
n.1: A pronoun stands in for a noun; "Yesterday" names the day directly.
n.3: An adjective describes a noun; "Yesterday" is the thing being described as "the busiest day."

q: In the sentence "That is the chart the surgeon asked for," what part of speech is the word "That"?
w: "That" stands alone as the subject of "is" and points to a thing, so it is a demonstrative pronoun.

n.0: "That" acts as an adjective only when a noun follows it ("That chart"); here no noun follows.
n.1: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; here "That" is the subject itself.
n.2: "That" is a conjunction when it introduces a clause ("She said that it was ready"); here it is the subject.

q: In the sentence "That chart belongs in the locked cabinet," what part of speech is the word "That"?
w: "That" points out which chart, so it modifies the noun "chart" and acts as an adjective.

n.0: "That" is a pronoun when it stands alone ("That belongs here"); here the noun "chart" follows it.
n.1: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "That" limits the noun "chart."
n.2: A conjunction joins clauses ("She said that it belongs here"); here "That" begins the subject.

q: In the sentence "After the shift ended, Rosa drove her coworker home," what part of speech is the word "After"?
w: "After" introduces the clause "the shift ended," which has a subject and a verb, so it is a subordinating conjunction.

n.0: "After" is a preposition when only a noun follows ("after the shift"); here a subject and verb follow.
n.1: An adjective describes a noun; "After" connects a time clause to the main clause.
n.3: "After" is an adverb when it stands alone ("She left soon after"); here it starts a clause.

q: In the sentence "Rosa drove home after her twelve-hour shift," what part of speech is the word "after"?
w: "After" takes the noun phrase "her twelve-hour shift" as its object, with no verb, so it is a preposition.

n.0: "Twelve-hour" is the adjective; "after" links the noun phrase to "drove."
n.1: "After" is an adverb only with no object ("soon after"); here it has the object "shift."
n.3: A subordinating conjunction is followed by a subject and a verb ("after her shift ended"); here only a noun phrase follows.

q: In the sentence "Everyone in the waiting room heard the announcement," what part of speech is the word "Everyone"?
w: "Everyone" is an indefinite pronoun: it stands in for people without naming them.

n.0: An adjective describes a noun; "Everyone" is the subject of "heard."
n.1: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; "Everyone" refers to people without naming any of them.
n.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "Everyone" is the subject.

q: In the sentence "The nurse gently lifted the crying toddler onto the exam table," what part of speech is the word "crying"?
w: "Crying" tells which toddler (the one who is crying), so this -ing form is a participle acting as an adjective that describes the noun "toddler."

n.0: An adverb would tell how the nurse lifted; "gently" does that job, while "crying" modifies the noun "toddler."
n.1: "Crying" has no helping verb (is, was), so it is not a verb here; the only verb in the sentence is "lifted."
n.3: An -ing form is a noun (a gerund) when it names an activity ("Crying tires a child"); here it describes "toddler."

q: In the sentence "The surgeon's hands stayed remarkably steady during the long operation," what part of speech is the word "remarkably"?
w: "Remarkably" modifies the adjective "steady," telling how steady, so it is an adverb.

n.0: A noun names something; "remarkably" tells to what degree.
n.1: "Steady" is the adjective; "remarkably" describes "steady," not a noun.
n.2: The verb is "stayed"; "remarkably" shows no action.

q: Which word in the sentence is a preposition? "Although the clinic closes early, the lab stays open until six."
w: "Until" takes the object "six" and has no verb after it, so it is a preposition showing time.

n.0: "Early" tells when the clinic closes, so it is an adverb.
n.1: "Although" is followed by a subject and verb ("the clinic closes"), so it is a subordinating conjunction.
n.3: "Open" follows the linking verb "stays" and describes the lab, so it is an adjective.

q: Which word in the sentence is an adverb? "The new nurse seemed nervous, yet she handled the emergency calmly."
w: "Calmly" tells how she handled the emergency, so it modifies the verb "handled" and is an adverb.

n.0: "New" describes the noun "nurse," so it is an adjective.
n.1: "Nervous" follows the linking verb "seemed" and describes the nurse, so it is an adjective.
n.2: "Yet" joins two independent clauses after a comma, so it is a coordinating conjunction here.

q: In the sentence "The patient did not eat breakfast, nor did he drink his juice," what part of speech is the word "nor"?
w: "Nor" is one of the coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS); here it joins two negative independent clauses.

n.0: A preposition takes a noun object; "nor" is followed by a full clause.
n.2: "Not" is the adverb in the first clause; "nor" links the two clauses.
n.3: A pronoun stands in for a noun; "nor" replaces no noun.

q: In the sentence "The aide handed the patient a cup of water," what is the function of "the patient"?
w: "The patient" tells to whom the cup was handed, so it is the indirect object. "A cup" is the direct object: the thing handed.

n.0: A subject complement follows a linking verb; "handed" is an action verb.
n.1: The direct object receives the action: the aide handed "a cup," not the patient.
n.2: No preposition comes before "the patient"; with one, it would read "to the patient."

q: In the sentence "Dr. Kim, the new cardiologist, starts on Monday," what is the function of "the new cardiologist"?
w: "The new cardiologist" is a noun phrase set off by commas that renames "Dr. Kim," so it is an appositive.

n.0: A subject complement follows a linking verb ("Dr. Kim is the new cardiologist"); no linking verb comes before this phrase.
n.1: The subject is "Dr. Kim"; the phrase only renames the subject.
n.2: "Starts" takes no object here; the phrase sits beside the subject, not after the verb.

q: In the sentence "Mr. Ortiz became a hospital volunteer after his recovery," what is the function of "a hospital volunteer"?
w: "Became" is a linking verb, and "a hospital volunteer" renames the subject, Mr. Ortiz, so it is a subject complement (a predicate noun).

n.0: A direct object receives an action; "became" is a linking verb, so nothing receives an action.
n.2: No preposition comes before the phrase; "his recovery" is the object of "after."
n.3: An indirect object tells to or for whom something is done; nothing is given here.

q: In the sentence "The nurse felt the patient's forehead for a fever," what kind of verb is "felt"?
w: The nurse performed an action on an object (the forehead), so "felt" is an action verb here.

n.0: An infinitive is "to" plus a verb ("to feel").
n.2: A helping verb supports a main verb ("has felt"); "felt" is the only verb.
n.3: "Felt" is a linking verb when a description of the subject follows ("The nurse felt tired"); here it has an object.

q: In the sentence "The patient has been resting quietly since noon," which word is the main verb?
w: In the verb phrase "has been resting," "has" and "been" are helping verbs; "resting" carries the main action.

n.0: "Been" is a helping verb here; it supports "resting."
n.1: "Has" is a helping verb that forms the perfect tense.
n.3: "Quietly" is an adverb telling how the patient was resting.

q: Which word in the sentence is an abstract noun? "The volunteer's patience comforted the frightened child."
w: "Patience" names a quality you cannot see or touch, so it is an abstract noun.

n.0: "Child" is a concrete noun: a person you can see.
n.2: "Frightened" describes the child, so it is an adjective.
n.3: "Volunteer's" is the possessive form of a concrete noun, a person you can see.

q: In the sentence "The extra gloves on the counter are hers," what part of speech is the word "hers"?
w: "Hers" stands alone in place of a noun phrase ("her gloves"), so it is a possessive pronoun.

n.0: "Her" acts as an adjective when a noun follows ("her gloves"); "hers" stands alone.
n.2: "Hers" replaces a noun phrase rather than naming something itself.
n.3: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; "hers" follows the linking verb "are" and stands for the owner's gloves.

q: Which sentence uses pronoun case correctly?
o: The award went to Devon and myself for the hand-hygiene project.
Between you and me, the new skills schedule is an improvement.
The instructor asked Maria and I to demonstrate the bed transfer.
Him and his sister both applied to the nursing program this year.
w: "Between" is a preposition, and the object of a preposition takes the objective case: "between you and me."

n.0: "Myself" is reflexive and has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Devon and me."
n.2: "Maria and I" is the object of "asked," so the objective case is needed: "asked Maria and me." Drop "Maria and" to test: "asked me."
n.3: "Him and his sister" is the subject, so the subjective case is needed: "He and his sister."

q: Which sentence uses "who" or "whom" correctly?
o: Whom do you think will be named the new charge nurse?
Whom is responsible for the night count of controlled drugs?
The student whom earned the top score will speak at graduation.
To whom should I send the completed insurance forms?
w: "Whom" is the objective form. In "To whom should I send," the pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (send them to him), so "whom" is correct.

n.0: Ignore "do you think": the pronoun is the subject of "will be named" (he will be named), so it must be "Who."
n.1: The pronoun is the subject of "is responsible" (he is responsible), so it must be "Who."
n.2: The pronoun is the subject of "earned" (she earned), so it must be "who."

q: Which sentence uses the pronoun "we" or "us" correctly?
o: The instructor gave us students extra time on the dosage exam.
Several of we applicants had questions about the essay prompt.
The new policy was explained to we volunteers on Monday.
Us students were asked to arrive by 6:30 a.m. for clinicals.
w: Drop the noun to test: "The instructor gave us extra time" is correct, so "gave us students" is correct. "Us" is the indirect object of "gave."

n.1: "Of" is a preposition, so its object needs the objective case: "several of us applicants."
n.2: Drop "volunteers": "explained to we" is wrong. The object of "to" needs "us volunteers."
n.3: Drop "students": "Us were asked" is wrong. The phrase is the subject, so it must be "We students."

q: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
o: The residents organized the whole fundraiser theirselves this year.
My lab partner and myself presented the case study on Monday.
Please return the signed form to Ms. Park or myself by Friday.
Kendra reminded herself to recheck the dosage before charting it.
w: A reflexive pronoun is correct when its antecedent is in the same clause. "Herself" refers back to "Kendra," who did the reminding.

n.0: "Theirselves" is nonstandard; the reflexive form is "themselves."
n.1: "Myself" cannot be part of a subject; the subjective case is needed: "My lab partner and I."
n.2: "Myself" has no antecedent in this sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Ms. Park or me."

q: Read the sentence: "The charge nurse divided the six patients between Tomas and I so that each of us had three." Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
w: "Between" is a preposition, so both of its objects take the objective case: "between Tomas and me."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so "had" (or "has") is right; "have" adds a tense shift and does not fix "between Tomas and I."
n.2: "Myself" needs an antecedent in the sentence that refers to the same person; the object of "between" needs "me."
n.3: "Us" is correct as the object of the preposition "of"; "each of we" would create a new error.

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Because the clinic has opened its second office, Dr. Liu and myself will divide our hours between the two sites."
w: "Dr. Liu and ___" is the subject of "will divide," so it needs the subjective "I": "Dr. Liu and I will divide our hours." "Myself" has no "I" earlier in the sentence to reflect.

n.0: "Our" correctly refers to Dr. Liu and the speaker together.
n.2: "Its" is the correct possessive for one clinic, written without an apostrophe.
n.3: "Between" is correct with two sites, and its object is a noun, not a pronoun.

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The instructor gave the extra study guide to Malik and ___."
w: "To" is a preposition, so its objects take the objective case. Drop test: "gave the guide to me," so "to Malik and me."

n.0: "Myself" needs an "I" earlier in the sentence to reflect; there is none.
n.2: "Mine" is a possessive pronoun; the guide was given to a person, not to something owned.
n.3: "Gave the guide to I" fails the drop test; "I" is subjective.

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The nurse to ___ the family wrote a thank-you letter has transferred to another unit."
w: The pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (the family wrote to her), so the objective "whom" is correct.

n.0: "Who" is subjective; directly after the preposition "to," the objective "whom" is needed.
n.1: "Whoever" is subjective and means "any person who"; the sentence refers to one known nurse.
n.2: "Whose" shows possession and would need a noun after it ("whose daughter").

q: Which sentence uses the correct pronoun in a compound subject?
o: Her and Tasha passed the dosage exam on the first try.
Tasha and her passed the dosage exam on the first try.
Tasha and she passed the dosage exam on the first try.
Tasha and herself passed the dosage exam on the first try.
w: The pair is the subject of "passed," so the subjective "she" is needed. Drop test: "She passed."

n.0: "Her passed" fails the drop test; the subject needs "She."
n.1: "Her" is objective; as part of the subject it must be "she."
n.3: "Herself" needs an antecedent in the same clause and cannot serve as a subject.

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The supervisor will give a parking pass to ___ needs one."
w: Inside its own clause the pronoun is the subject of "needs" (he needs one), so "whoever" is correct. The whole clause "whoever needs one" is the object of "to."

n.0: "Whose" shows possession and would need a noun after it.
n.2: "Whomever" is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of "needs"; the preposition governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.
n.3: "Whom" is objective and cannot be the subject of "needs."

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "Jada has worked more night shifts this year than ___ have."
w: Finish the comparison: "than I have." The pronoun is the subject of "have," so the subjective "I" is correct.

n.0: "Her have" fails: the subject form is "she," and "she" would also need "has."
n.1: "Than me have" fails: "me" cannot be the subject of "have."
n.3: "Myself" is reflexive and cannot be the subject of "have."

q: Which sentence uses a possessive pronoun correctly?
o: Is the stethoscope on the counter your's?
The blue lunch bag on the top shelf is her's.
The final decision about surgery was theirs.
The clinic updated it's visiting hours today.
w: Possessive pronouns (hers, theirs, its, yours) take no apostrophe, so "theirs" is correct.

n.0: "Your's" is not a standard form; the possessive pronoun is "yours."
n.1: "Her's" is not a standard form; the possessive pronoun is "hers."
n.3: "It's" means "it is"; the possessive is "its": "updated its visiting hours."

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The orientation leader asked ___ new hires to wait in the lobby."
w: Drop the noun: "asked us to wait." The pronoun is the object of "asked," so the objective "us" is correct.

n.1: "Asked we" fails the drop test; "we" is subjective.
n.2: "Ourselves" is reflexive and needs "we" as the subject of the same clause.
n.3: "Them" cannot point to a noun; "them new hires" is nonstandard.

q: Which revision of "When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he explained the test results" removes the unclear pronoun reference?
o: When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he carefully explained the test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, they explained the new test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, the doctor explained the test results.
Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, and he explained all of the new test results.
w: A pronoun must point to one clear antecedent. Replacing "he" with "the doctor" shows that Dr. Okafor explained the results.

n.0: Adding "carefully" does not fix the problem: "he" could still mean either man.
n.1: "They" is still unclear (both men? someone else?) and does not identify who explained the results.
n.3: Joining the clauses with "and" keeps the same ambiguous "he" with two possible antecedents.

q: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun reference?
o: The employee handbook states that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
The handbook and the shift schedule both list breaks, and it says they last thirty minutes.
They say in the employee handbook that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
In the employee handbook, they state that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
w: Every pronoun needs a clear antecedent. Making "the employee handbook" the subject removes the vague "they" or "it."

n.1: "It" could mean the handbook or the shift schedule, so the reference is unclear even though both nouns are named.
n.2: "They" has no antecedent; the sentence never names who "they" are.
n.3: "They" is vague: the handbook is a thing, and no people have been named.

q: Which revision of "The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had been changed" makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The pharmacist and the technician were told that her shift changed.
The pharmacist told the technician, "Your shift has been changed."
The pharmacist told the technician that her own shift had been changed.
The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had now been changed.
w: Turning the report into a direct quotation makes "your" refer clearly to the technician, the person being spoken to.

n.0: "Her" now has two possible antecedents in the subject, so the reference is still unclear.
n.2: Adding "own" does not help: "her own" could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.
n.3: Adding "now" leaves "her" ambiguous; it could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.

q: Which revision of "When the nurse set the vial on the tray, it cracked" removes the unclear pronoun reference?
o: When the nurse set the vial on the tray, they cracked.
The nurse set the vial on the tray, and it cracked.
The vial cracked when the nurse set it on the tray.
When the nurse set the vial on the tray, it suddenly cracked.
w: With "the vial" named as the subject, "it" has one possible antecedent: the vial.

n.0: "They" has no plural antecedent and still does not say what cracked.
n.1: Joining the clauses with "and" keeps "it" pointing to either the vial or the tray.
n.3: Adding "suddenly" leaves "it" pointing to either the vial or the tray.

q: Which sentence about exam preparation avoids a shift in pronoun person?
o: If one studies daily, you will feel ready for the exam.
If students study daily, they will feel ready for the exam.
If students study daily, we will feel ready for the exam.
If a student studies daily, you will feel ready for the exam.
w: "Students" and "they" are both third person plural, so person and number stay consistent.

n.0: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to second person ("you").
n.2: The sentence shifts from third person ("students") to first person ("we").
n.3: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you").

q: Which revision of "At the clinic, they told me to fast before the blood test" corrects the vague pronoun?
o: The clinic nurse told me to fast before the blood test.
At the clinic, it told me to fast before the blood test.
They told me at the clinic to fast before the blood test.
At the clinic, they told me that I should fast before the test.
w: "They" has no antecedent; naming "the clinic nurse" tells the reader who gave the instruction.

n.1: "It" is still vague, and a clinic building cannot give instructions.
n.2: Moving the phrase does not give "they" an antecedent.
n.3: Rewording the rest of the sentence leaves "they" without an antecedent.

q: Which revision of "Mr. Ross told his son that his test results were normal" makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: Mr. Ross told his son that his own test results were normal.
Mr. Ross told his son, "Your test results are normal."
Mr. Ross told his son that his recent test results were normal.
Mr. Ross and his son were told that his test results were normal.
w: In the direct quotation, "your" can only mean the son, the person being spoken to, so only one reading is possible.

n.0: "His own" could still mean the father's results or the son's.
n.2: Adding "recent" leaves "his" pointing to either man.
n.3: "His" now has two possible antecedents in the subject.

q: Which sentence contains a pronoun with no clear antecedent?
o: In the brochure, it says that flu shots are free.
Dr. Ames said she would give the flu shots herself.
The brochure says that flu shots are free for staff.
The clinic posted its flu-shot hours on the door.
w: "It" has no noun to refer to; the brochure is the source, so name it: "The brochure says..."

n.1: "She" and "herself" both clearly refer to Dr. Ames.
n.2: The brochure is named as the subject, so no pronoun needs an antecedent.
n.3: "Its" clearly refers to the clinic.

q: Which word in the sentence has an unclear antecedent? "When Ella handed Dana the report, which had just arrived, she noticed that its last page was missing."
w: "She" could mean Ella or Dana, so its antecedent is unclear. "Which" and "its" can refer only to the report.

n.1: "Its" can refer only to the report, the one thing in the sentence that has pages.
n.2: "That" after "noticed" is a conjunction introducing a clause, not a pronoun, so it has no antecedent.
n.3: "Which" comes right after "the report" and can refer only to it.

q: Which revision of "When one starts a new job, you often feel nervous" corrects the shift in person?
o: When one starts a new job, we often feel nervous.
When you start a new job, you often feel nervous.
When you start a new job, one often feels nervous.
When one starts a new job, I often feel nervous.
w: "You ... you" keeps the same (second) person throughout. ("One ... one" would also be consistent.)

n.0: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to first person ("we").
n.2: The shift is reversed: second person ("you") to third person ("one").
n.3: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to first person ("I").

q: Which revision of "Ty wants to be a nurse because it is a rewarding career" corrects the vague pronoun?
o: Ty wants to be a nurse because that is a rewarding career.
Ty wants to be a nurse because nursing is a rewarding career.
Ty wants to be a nurse because they have a rewarding career.
Ty wants to be a nurse, and it is a rewarding career.
w: "It" has no noun to stand for: the sentence names "a nurse" (a person), not "nursing" (a career). Naming "nursing" fixes the reference.

n.0: "That" is just as vague: no noun in the sentence names the career.
n.2: "They" has no plural antecedent; the only people named are Ty and "a nurse."
n.3: Joining the clauses with "and" still leaves "it" with no noun to refer to.

q: Which revision of "The nurses told the patients that they would be moved to the new wing" makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The nurses told the patients, "You will be moved to the new wing."
The nurses told the patients that they would be moved to their new wing.
The patients were told by the nurses that they would be moved to the new wing.
The nurses told the patients that they would all be moved to the new wing.
w: In the quotation, "you" can only mean the patients, the people being spoken to, so the reference is clear.

n.1: "They" and "their" could each mean the nurses or the patients.
n.2: Switching to the passive voice keeps "they" with two possible antecedents.
n.3: Adding "all" leaves "they" pointing to either the nurses or the patients.

q: Which of these sentences has a clear pronoun reference?
o: On the hospital website, they list the visiting hours for each unit.
Before Leo met Sam at the clinic, he had not had a flu shot.
Kara called Mia after the shift, and she was exhausted.
Kara was exhausted when she called Mia after the shift.
w: "She" is the subject of "called," and the person called is Mia, so "she" can only mean Kara.

n.0: "They" has no antecedent; name the source ("The hospital website lists...").
n.1: "He" could mean Leo or Sam.
n.2: "She" could mean Kara or Mia.

q: Which sentence keeps verb tense consistent?
o: The aide weighed the patient and writes the result on the board.
The aide weighs the patient and wrote the result on the board.
The aide weighed the patient and wrote the result on the board.
The aide weighs the patient and had written the result on the board.
w: Both actions happened in the same past visit, so both verbs stay in the simple past: "weighed ... wrote."

n.0: The sentence shifts from past ("weighed") to present ("writes") for two actions in the same visit.
n.1: The sentence shifts from present ("weighs") to past ("wrote") with no change in time.
n.3: The past perfect "had written" places the writing before the weighing, which is illogical, and it clashes with the present "weighs."

q: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?
o: The surgeon finishes the procedure by the time the family had arrived.
The surgeon has finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrives.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
w: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. The procedure ended first, then the family arrived.

n.0: The tenses are reversed: the earlier action (finishing) needs the past perfect, and the later one the simple past.
n.1: The present perfect "has finished" does not fit a completed past time frame set by "arrived"; use "had finished."
n.2: "Arrives" is present tense, which clashes with "had finished"; both events are in the past.

q: In formal written English, which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
o: If I were the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I would be the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I was the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I will allow one retake per exam.
w: For an unreal or hypothetical condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects and "would" in the main clause.

n.1: "Would" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause; use "If I were."
n.2: A condition contrary to fact takes the subjunctive "were" in formal writing, not "was."
n.3: An unreal "if I were" condition pairs with "would," not the future "will."

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic, where she checks in patients and took their blood pressure."
w: The sentence describes last spring, so every verb stays in the past. "Checks" jumps to the present; it should be "checked," to match "volunteered" and "took."

n.1: "Volunteered" is simple past, which matches "Last spring."
n.2: "Their" is the correct possessive for the patients.
n.3: "Took" is the simple past of "take," which fits the past time frame.

q: Which sentence uses verb tense correctly with the phrase "since 2019"?
o: Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital in 2019.
Dr. Patel works at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel is working at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital since 2019.
w: The present perfect (has/have + past participle) shows an action that began in the past and continues now: "has worked ... since 2019."

n.0: The present perfect does not pair with a finished, specific past time such as "in 2019"; use "worked in 2019."
n.1: "Since" marks an action that began in the past and continues, which needs the present perfect "has worked."
n.2: The present progressive does not fit an ongoing span that began at a past point; use "has worked" or "has been working."

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "By the end of next May, Lena ___ all of her prerequisite courses."
w: The future perfect (will have + past participle) shows an action that will be finished before a future time ("by the end of next May").

n.0: The past perfect marks an action before another past event, but next May is still ahead.
n.2: "Would have completed" belongs in a condition contrary to fact ("If she had enrolled, she would have completed..."); the sentence states a plan.
n.3: The present perfect connects the past to now; it cannot be finished by a future date.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Mr. Lee ___ when the fire alarm sounded at 2 a.m."
w: The past progressive (was + -ing) shows an action in progress in the past when another past action ("sounded") interrupted it.

n.0: The present perfect progressive runs up to now, but the alarm sounded at a finished past moment.
n.1: The simple present describes habits or facts and clashes with the past "sounded."
n.2: The present progressive shows an action happening now, which clashes with the past "sounded."

q: Read the sentence: "When the doctor enters the room, the patient sat up in bed." Which revision corrects the tense error?
w: Both actions happen in the same time frame. Matching "sat" to the present "enters" gives "When the doctor enters the room, the patient sits up in bed."

n.1: English uses the present tense, not "will," after "when" in a time clause, and the clash with "sat" would remain.
n.2: "Has sat" is the present perfect, a finished action, which still does not match the habit shown by "enters."
n.3: "Sitting" without a helping verb cannot be the main verb, so the main clause would have no complete verb.

q: Which of these sentences is in the active voice?
o: The charts were reviewed by the night nurse.
The night nurse reviewed the charts at noon.
The samples had been labeled by the technician.
The new policy was announced by the director.
w: In the active voice the subject does the action: the night nurse (subject) reviewed the charts.

n.0: The subject "charts" receives the action ("were reviewed"), so this is passive voice.
n.2: The subject "samples" receives the action ("had been labeled"), so this is passive voice.
n.3: The subject "policy" receives the action ("was announced"), so this is passive voice.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Ms. Grant ___ her CPR certification last March."
w: "Last March" names a finished past time, so the simple past "renewed" is correct.

n.0: The simple present describes habits or facts now, not a single action last March.
n.1: The present perfect progressive describes an action continuing up to now, which clashes with "last March."
n.2: The present perfect does not pair with a finished, specific past time such as "last March."

q: Which verb phrase correctly completes the sentence? "If the lab had called sooner, the nurse ___ the dose."
w: A past condition contrary to fact uses "had" + past participle in the if-clause and "would have" + past participle in the result clause.

n.0: "Would of" is a mishearing of "would've"; "of" is not a verb.
n.2: "Had" + participle belongs in the if-clause; the result clause needs "would have changed."
n.3: "Will have changed" is the future perfect and cannot follow a past unreal condition.

q: Which verb phrase correctly completes the sentence? "If the nurse ___ about the allergy, she would have chosen a different antibiotic."
w: For an unreal past condition, the if-clause takes the past perfect: "If the nurse had known..., she would have chosen..."

n.0: "Would have" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause ("if I would have known" is a common error).
n.2: "Would know" does not belong in an if-clause and does not show past time.
n.3: The present perfect does not fit an unreal past condition.

q: Which sentence changes tense correctly because the time actually changes?
o: Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
Last year Omar has volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he worked there.
Omar volunteers at the clinic last year, and now he works there.
w: "Last year" calls for the past ("volunteered"), and "now" calls for the present ("works"): the tense changes because the time changes.

n.1: The present perfect "has volunteered" does not pair with the finished time "last year."
n.2: "Now" is present time, so the past "worked" is wrong.
n.3: "Last year" is past time, so the present "volunteers" is wrong.

q: Which sentence uses the correct form of an irregular verb?
o: She has wrote three care plans for the pediatric rotation.
I seen the updated schedule posted near the break room.
By the time I arrived, my preceptor had went to the meeting.
The new aide has already taken the medication safety course.
w: "Take" is irregular: take, took, taken. A helping verb ("has") takes the past participle "taken."

n.0: "Has" needs the past participle "written"; "wrote" is the simple past.
n.1: "Seen" is a past participle and needs a helping verb ("have seen"); otherwise use the simple past "saw."
n.2: "Had" needs the past participle "gone"; "went" is the simple past and cannot follow a helping verb.

q: Which sentence uses "lie" or "lay" correctly?
o: The dog has laid by the front door all afternoon long.
Please lie the clean linens on the bottom shelf of the cart.
After the procedure, the patient laid on his side for an hour.
Yesterday, Ana lay down for a nap after her long night shift.
w: "Lie" (to recline, no object) is lie, lay, lain. "Yesterday ... lay down" is the past tense of "lie," so it is correct.

n.0: The dog is reclining, so the verb is "lie"; its past participle is "lain": "has lain."
n.1: Putting linens down takes an object, so the verb is "lay": "Please lay the clean linens."
n.2: The patient is reclining (no object), so the verb is "lie"; its past tense is "lay," not "laid."

q: Which sentence uses "rise" or "raise" correctly?
o: The patient's temperature rose overnight, so we called the doctor.
The therapist asked the patient to rise his arm above his head.
The aide raised from her chair when the surgeon entered the room.
Prices for the required nursing textbooks have raised every semester.
w: "Rise" (rise, rose, risen) has no object; "raise" (raise, raised, raised) takes one. A temperature goes up by itself, so "rose" is correct.

n.1: Lifting an arm takes an object ("his arm"), so the verb must be "raise."
n.2: Getting up has no object, so the verb must be "rose" (past of "rise").
n.3: Prices go up on their own (no object), so the verb must be "risen": "have risen."

q: Which sentence uses "sit" and "set" correctly?
o: Please set in the chair by the window until your name is called.
The patient has set in the waiting room for over two hours.
She sat the specimen cup on the counter next to the sink.
He set the tray on the table and sat beside his mother.
w: "Set" (set, set, set) means to place something and takes an object (the tray). "Sit" (sit, sat, sat) has no object (he sat).

n.0: A person resting in a chair needs "sit" (no object); "set" means to place something.
n.1: The patient is seated (no object), so the verb must be "sat": "has sat."
n.2: Placing a cup takes an object, so the verb must be "set": "She set the specimen cup."

q: Read the sentence: "Since the new reminder policy started, the clinic has saw fewer missed appointments." Which revision corrects the verb error?
w: Two steps: "since" calls for the present perfect, and a singular subject ("clinic") takes "has" + the past participle "seen."

n.0: "Saw" is the simple past and cannot follow any helping verb; the participle is "seen."
n.1: "Seen" is right, but "clinic" is singular, so the helping verb must stay "has."
n.2: A past participle cannot stand alone as the main verb; it needs "has."

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The patient has ___ in bed since breakfast."
w: The patient is reclining (no object), so the verb is "lie": lie, lay, lain. After "has," use the past participle "lain."

n.0: "Laid" is the past participle of "lay" (to put something down) and needs an object.
n.2: "Lay" is the simple past of "lie" and cannot follow "has."
n.3: "Lied" is the past of "lie" meaning to tell an untruth.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Before the exam began, Ms. Ruiz ___ her photo ID on the proctor's desk."
w: Putting the ID down takes an object ("her photo ID"), so the verb is "lay," and its simple past is "laid."

n.0: "Layed" is not a standard form; the past of "lay" is "laid."
n.1: "Lay" here would be the past of "lie" (to recline), which takes no object.
n.2: "Lain" is the past participle of "lie" and needs a helping verb.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the night shift began, the moon had already ___."
w: The moon goes up by itself (no object), so the verb is "rise": rise, rose, risen. After "had," use "risen."

n.0: "Rise" is irregular; "rised" is not a standard form.
n.2: "Rose" is the simple past and cannot follow "had."
n.3: "Raised" is a form of "raise," which needs an object (raise something).

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The water in the specimen cooler had ___ solid overnight."
w: Freeze, froze, frozen: after "had," use the past participle "frozen."

n.0: "Froze" is the simple past and cannot follow "had."
n.1: "Had freezing" is not a verb form; the progressive would need "had been freezing."
n.3: "Freeze" is irregular; "freezed" is not a standard form.

q: Which sentence uses the correct past or past participle form?
o: The volunteer brung extra blankets to the shelter.
The phone rang twice before the nurse answered it.
The bell had rang twice before the class started.
The toddler had tore the paper gown into pieces.
w: "Rang" is the simple past of "ring" and stands alone without a helping verb.

n.0: "Brung" is nonstandard; the past of "bring" is "brought."
n.2: After "had," the past participle "rung" is needed: "had rung."
n.3: After "had," the past participle "torn" is needed: "had torn."

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The guest speaker has ___ about patient safety at every orientation since 2022."
w: Speak, spoke, spoken: after "has," use the past participle "spoken."

n.0: "Spoke" is the simple past and cannot follow "has."
n.2: "Speak" is irregular; "speaked" is not a standard form.
n.3: "Speak" is the base form and cannot follow "has."

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "The patient sat in the chair while the aide raised the bed and lay a clean sheet over the mattress."
w: Putting a sheet down takes an object, so the verb is "lay," whose past tense is "laid": "laid a clean sheet." "Lay" is the past of "lie," which takes no object.

n.0: "Over" is a correct preposition showing where the sheet went.
n.2: "Sat" is the correct past of "sit"; the patient took a seat, with no object.
n.3: "Raised" is correct: the aide lifted something (the bed).

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Before measuring the dose, the nurse had ___ the bottle well."
w: Shake, shook, shaken: after "had," use the past participle "shaken."

n.1: "Shake" is the base form and cannot follow "had."
n.2: "Shake" is irregular; "shaked" is not a standard form.
n.3: "Shook" is the simple past and cannot follow "had."

q: Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
o: The team did good on the state safety inspection this year.
The new graduate handled the emergency calm and careful.
After a night of rest, Jordan felt well enough to go to class.
The cafeteria soup tasted differently after the new cook started.
w: "Well" can be an adjective meaning "in good health," so "felt well" is correct after the linking verb "felt."

n.0: "Did" is an action verb here, so it needs the adverb "well": "did well on the inspection."
n.1: "Calm" and "careful" describe how she handled it, so they modify a verb and must be adverbs: "calmly and carefully."
n.3: "Tasted" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective that describes the soup: "tasted different."

q: Which sentence uses a comparative or superlative form correctly?
o: Of the two inhalers, the blue one is the most effective for her asthma.
Of the three textbooks, this one is the better choice for anatomy.
The night shift is more busier than the day shift on most weekends.
Of the three dressings, the foam one is the least painful to remove.
w: With three or more items, use the superlative (-est, most, least). Three dressings are compared, so "least painful" is correct.

n.0: Comparing exactly two items calls for the comparative: "the more effective."
n.1: Comparing three or more items calls for the superlative: "the best choice."
n.2: "More busier" is a double comparative; use "busier" alone.

q: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
o: Their new manager seems nicely, and the staff likes her a lot.
The coffee in the staff break room tastes bitter today.
The infant is breathing good now that the fever has broken.
The new bandage feels tightly around her swollen wrist.
w: Linking verbs (taste, seem, feel, look, smell) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it: the coffee tastes bitter.

n.0: "Seems" is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective "nice," not the adverb "nicely."
n.2: "Breathing" is an action, so it needs the adverb "well," not the adjective "good."
n.3: "Feels" links the bandage to a description of it, so it takes the adjective "tight," not the adverb "tightly."

q: Which sentence uses "good" or "well" correctly?
o: The team performed good during the mock code drill.
Ms. Dorsey sang well at the hospital fundraiser.
The incision is healing good, so the stitches can come out.
The new monitor works good once it is calibrated.
w: "Sang" is an action verb, so it takes the adverb "well."

n.0: "Performed" is an action verb and needs the adverb "well."
n.2: "Healing" is an action and needs the adverb "well": "is healing well."
n.3: "Works" is an action verb and needs the adverb "well": "works well."

q: Which sentence uses "bad" or "badly" correctly?
o: The new aide wrote the report bad and had to redo it.
The runner sprained her ankle bad during the race.
The patient's cough sounded bad last night.
The patient slept bad because of the noisy hallway.
w: "Sounded" is a linking verb here: it connects the cough to a description, so it takes the adjective "bad."

n.0: "Wrote" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."
n.1: "Sprained" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."
n.3: "Slept" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Of the four practice tests, the third one gave Hana her ___ score."
w: Four tests are compared, so the superlative of "bad" is needed: bad, worse, worst.

n.0: "Bad" is irregular; "baddest" is not standard in formal English.
n.1: "Most worst" is a double superlative; "worst" already means "most bad."
n.3: "Worse" is the comparative, used for exactly two items.

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The nurse spoke ___ to the frightened child before the blood draw."
w: "Spoke" is an action verb, so the word that tells how she spoke must be an adverb: "gently."

n.0: "Gentle" is an adjective; it can describe a person or a touch but not the action "spoke."
n.1: "Gentlest" is a superlative adjective, and nothing is being compared or described.
n.2: "Gentleness" is a noun; it would need "with" before it ("spoke with gentleness").

q: Which sentence uses the articles "a" and "an" correctly?
o: The aide waited a hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering a uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering a uniform.
w: The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) and "a uniform" (begins with a "you" consonant sound).

n.0: Both are reversed: "an hour" and "a uniform".
n.2: "Uniform" begins with a consonant "y" sound, so it takes "a".
n.3: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an".

q: Read the sentence: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.1: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.
n.2: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."

q: Which sentence is written in standard English with no double negative?
o: The aide hadn't scarcely finished charting when the call light came on.
The patient can't hardly sit up in bed without help from staff.
The pharmacy didn't have any of the brand-name tablets in stock.
There isn't no reason for the patient to skip the follow-up visit.
w: One negative is enough. "Didn't" is negative and "any" is neutral, so the sentence is correct.

n.0: "Scarcely" is negative in meaning, so "hadn't scarcely" is a double negative; use "had scarcely."
n.1: "Hardly" is already negative, so "can't hardly" is a double negative; use "can hardly."
n.3: "Isn't" and "no" are two negatives; use "There is no reason" or "There isn't any reason."

q: Which of these sentences is written in standard English?
o: Them forms need a signature from the patient or parent.
Irregardless of the forecast, the clinic will open at eight.
The clinic use to open at seven on weekday mornings.
The aide was supposed to restock the gloves before noon.
w: "Was supposed to" is the standard written form: "supposed" keeps its -d ending.

n.0: "Them" cannot point to a noun; use "Those forms."
n.1: "Irregardless" is nonstandard; use "regardless."
n.2: The past-habit form needs the -d ending in writing: "used to open."

q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? "Ms. Park learned ___ about wound care during her first clinical rotation."
w: "A lot" (a great deal) is written as two words.

n.1: "Alot" is not standard English; write "a lot."
n.2: "Allot" is a verb meaning to give out shares ("allot time"), which does not fit after "learned."
n.3: "Lot" stays singular in this phrase: "a lot," not "a lots."

q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? "Please hand me ___ gloves from the top shelf."
w: "Those" is the standard word for pointing to things at a distance (on the top shelf).

n.0: "Them there" stacks two nonstandard pointing words; use "those."
n.1: "These here" adds an unneeded "here"; standard English uses "these" or "those" alone.
n.2: "Them" is an object pronoun and cannot point to a noun; "them gloves" is nonstandard.

q: Which sentence uses "their," "there" and "they're" correctly?
o: Their leaving their coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over their by the door.
They're leaving there coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over there by the door.
w: "They're" is the contraction of "they are", "their" shows possession (their coats), and "there" names a place (over there).

n.0: The sentence needs "they are leaving", so the contraction "they're" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.1: "Over ___" names a place, so "there" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.2: The coats belong to them, so the possessive "their" is required, not the place word "there".

q: Which sentence uses "than" and "then" correctly?
o: The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
w: "Than" makes a comparison (longer than expected); "then" shows time or sequence (and then left).

n.0: Both are reversed: the comparison needs "than" and the sequence needs "then".
n.1: "And ___ left" shows sequence, so it needs "then".
n.2: "Longer ___ expected" is a comparison, so it needs "than".

q: Which sentence uses "to," "too" and "two" correctly?
o: The two aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were to tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were too tired too finish the charts.
The too aides were too tired to finish the charts.
w: "Two" is the number, "too" means excessively (too tired), and "to" begins the infinitive (to finish).

n.1: "___ tired" means excessively tired, which requires "too".
n.2: An infinitive is formed with "to": "to finish".
n.3: The number of aides requires "two".

q: Which sentence uses "who's" and "whose" correctly?
o: Who's the patient whose chart is missing?
Who's the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient whose chart is missing?
Whose the patient who's chart is missing?
w: "Who's" is the contraction of "who is" (Who is the patient?); "whose" shows possession (whose chart).

n.1: The chart belongs to the patient, so the possessive "whose" is needed, not "who is".
n.2: The sentence opens with "Who is the patient", so it needs the contraction "who's".
n.3: Both are reversed: the opening needs "who's" and the possessive needs "whose".

q: Which sentence uses "affect" and "effect" correctly?
o: The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
w: "Affect" is usually a verb meaning "to influence" (did not affect her sleep); "effect" is usually a noun meaning "result" (an effect on her appetite).

n.0: After the article "an", the noun meaning "result" is needed: "effect".
n.1: "Did not ___ her sleep" needs the verb meaning "influence", which is "affect"; "effect" as a verb means "bring about".
n.3: Both are reversed: the verb should be "affect" and the noun should be "effect".

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The school's ____ explained that honesty is a basic ____ of the honor code."
w: "Principal" names the head of a school (or means "main"); "principle" is a rule or belief, as in a principle of the honor code.

n.0: A basic rule of a code is a "principle", not a "principal".
n.2: The head of a school is the "principal", not a "principle".
n.3: Both words are reversed: the school's head is the principal, and a rule is a principle.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new exercise bike is ____, so it will ____ the walking program."
w: "Stationary" means not moving; "complement" means to complete or go well with. A bike that stays in place goes well with a walking program.

n.0: "Stationery" is writing paper; a bike that does not move is "stationary".
n.2: "Compliment" means to praise; going well with something is "complement".
n.3: Both are wrong: the bike is stationary (not moving), and it complements (goes well with) the program.

q: Which sentence uses the commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".
n.3: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the instruction? "The respiratory therapist will ____ you to take a deep ____ before you exhale slowly."
w: "Advise" is the verb (will advise you); "breath" is the noun (a deep breath). "Advice" and "breathe" are the noun and verb forms of the other pair.

n.0: After "a deep" a noun is needed: "breath". "Breathe" is a verb.
n.1: Both are reversed: the verb is "advise" and the noun is "breath".
n.2: After "will" a verb is needed: "advise". "Advice" is a noun.

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "The council decided that the new policy would affect personnel who leave there stations early."
w: The stations belong to the personnel, so the possessive "their" is required: "leave their stations."

n.0: "Council" (a group that makes decisions) is correct; "counsel" means advice.
n.1: "Personnel" (staff) is correct; "personal" means private.
n.3: "Affect" is correct: after "would" a verb meaning "to influence" is needed, and "effect" is usually a noun.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the team was ____ to begin, the patient had ____ been discharged."
w: "All ready" means completely prepared (the team was all ready to begin); "already" means by this time (had already been discharged).

n.1: "Had all ready been discharged" needs the time word "already".
n.2: Both are reversed: being prepared is "all ready", and "by this time" is "already".
n.3: Being completely prepared is "all ready"; "was already to begin" does not make sense.

q: Which sentence about the clinic website uses "its" and "it's" correctly?
o: It's time to update the clinic and it's website.
Its time to update the clinic and its website.
It's time to update the clinic and its website.
Its time to update the clinic and it's website.
w: "It's" means "it is" (It is time); "its" is the possessive (the clinic's website is its website).

n.0: The possessive needs "its" with no apostrophe; "it's website" would mean "it is website."
n.1: "It is time" needs the contraction "It's."
n.3: Both are reversed: "It is time" needs "It's," and the possessive needs "its."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "Although he was fully ___ during the procedure, his guilty ___ kept him from admitting he had eaten breakfast."
w: "Conscious" (adjective) means awake and aware; "conscience" (noun) is a person's moral sense, which can feel guilty.

n.1: A guilty moral sense is a "conscience"; "conscious" is an adjective and cannot follow "his guilty."
n.2: Being awake is "conscious"; "conscience" is a noun and cannot describe how he was.
n.3: Both are reversed: being awake is "conscious," and a guilty moral sense is a "conscience."

q: Which sentence uses "fewer" or "less" correctly?
o: There were fewer complaints after the new check-in system began.
The clinic saw less patients this month than it did last month.
The new menu offers less calories per serving than the old one did.
The weekend shift now runs with less staff members than before.
w: Use "fewer" with countable plural nouns (complaints, patients, calories, staff members) and "less" with uncountable nouns (water, sodium, time).

n.1: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer patients."
n.2: "Calories" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer calories."
n.3: "Staff members" is a countable plural, so it needs "fewer staff members" ("less staff" alone would be fine).

q: Which sentence uses "number" or "amount" correctly?
o: The amount of volunteers at the blood drive doubled this year.
The large amount of patients in the lobby slowed down check-in.
A large number of applicants missed the deadline this year.
The nurse charted the number of fluid the patient drank.
w: "Number" goes with countable plural nouns (applicants, patients, volunteers); "amount" goes with uncountable nouns (fluid, water, paperwork).

n.0: "Volunteers" are countable, so the sentence needs "number of volunteers."
n.1: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "number," not "amount."
n.3: Fluid cannot be counted one by one, so the sentence needs "the amount of fluid."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The surgeon did not say it directly, but she ___ that surgery was likely, and the family ___ the same thing from her tone."
w: The speaker implies (suggests); the listener infers (concludes). The surgeon implied it, and the family inferred it.

n.0: Both are reversed: the speaker suggests (implies) and the listeners conclude (infer).
n.1: The surgeon suggested the idea, so she "implied" it; inferring is what the listener does.
n.2: The family drew a conclusion, so they "inferred"; implying is what the speaker does.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new meal plan calls for ___ sodium and ___ processed snacks each day."
w: Sodium is uncountable, so "less sodium"; snacks can be counted, so "fewer processed snacks."

n.0: Sodium cannot be counted one by one, so it takes "less," not "fewer."
n.1: Both are reversed: uncountable sodium takes "less," and countable snacks take "fewer."
n.3: "Snacks" is a countable plural, so it takes "fewer," not "less."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "A large ___ of visitors left a surprising ___ of trash in the lobby."
w: Visitors can be counted ("number of visitors"); trash cannot ("amount of trash").

n.0: Both are reversed: countable visitors take "number," and uncountable trash takes "amount."
n.2: Visitors are countable, so they take "number," not "amount."
n.3: Trash is uncountable, so it takes "amount," not "number."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The ___ cardiologist warned the family that the patient's heart failure was ___."
w: "Eminent" means distinguished or well known; "imminent" means about to happen.

n.0: Both are reversed: a distinguished doctor is "eminent," and an event about to happen is "imminent."
n.2: Heart failure that is about to happen is "imminent," not "eminent."
n.3: A distinguished cardiologist is "eminent"; "imminent" describes events, not people.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The counselor's open questions helped ___ honest answers about the teen's ___ drug use."
w: "Elicit" is a verb meaning to draw out; "illicit" is an adjective meaning illegal.

n.0: After "helped," a verb meaning to draw out is needed: "elicit."
n.2: An adjective meaning illegal is needed before "drug use": "illicit."
n.3: Both are reversed: "helped ___ answers" needs the verb "elicit," and illegal drug use is "illicit."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "Hospital ___ may not keep ___ belongings in the medication room."
w: "Personnel" means staff; "personal" means belonging to a particular person.

n.1: The staff of a hospital are its "personnel," a noun.
n.2: Belongings that are one's own are "personal," not "personnel."
n.3: Both are reversed: staff are "personnel," and a person's own belongings are "personal."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The city ___ hired a lawyer to ___ its members on the new public health code."
w: A "council" is a governing group; "counsel" as a verb means to advise.

n.1: A city's governing group is a "council."
n.2: After "to," a verb meaning advise is needed: "counsel."
n.3: Both are reversed: the governing group is a "council," and to advise is to "counsel."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "In her note, the nurse described redness at the IV ___ and ___ the hospital policy on dressing changes."
w: A "site" is a location (the IV site); to "cite" is to refer to a source, so the past tense is "cited."

n.1: "Cite" is a verb, not a location, and "sited" means placed; the words are reversed.
n.2: "Sighted" means saw; referring to a policy is "cited."
n.3: "Sight" means vision; a location on the body is a "site."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The coordinator asked ___ the stormy ___ would delay the blood drive."
w: "Whether" introduces a possibility ("if"); "weather" is the condition of the air outside.

n.1: Both are reversed: "asked ___" needs "whether," and the storm is "weather."
n.2: "Stormy ___" names conditions outside: "weather."
n.3: "Asked ___ the ... would" needs the word meaning "if": "whether."

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The volunteer ___ greeted us at the entrance has worked here for ten years."
w: "Who" refers to people and is the subject of "greeted," so it is correct.

n.1: "Which" refers to things or animals, not to a person such as a volunteer.
n.2: "Whose" shows possession and would need a noun after it.
n.3: "Whom" is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of "greeted."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The nurses gathered ___ in the lounge, but the meeting ran ___ too long."
w: "All together" means as a group; "altogether" means completely.

n.0: The word meaning "completely" is one word: "altogether too long."
n.2: Both are reversed: gathering as a group is "all together," and "completely too long" is "altogether too long."
n.3: Gathering as one group is "all together," two words.
